headline: When states override environmental law, the environment has no government
context: Malaysia's Constitution does not define 'environment.' DOE can object but states can override. Parliament passed forest protection reforms in 2022. By March 2025, they were in force only in Perlis and the Federal Territories.

changes.summary: Correction: The hook now says 42 people died at sites where EIA rules were overridden, instead of in landslides "linked to EIA bypass".

Correction: Earlier editions said 42 people died at sites where environmental rules were overridden and that most were low-income and migrant workers; that holds only for the 11 construction workers killed at Tanjung Bungah, on a project the DOE had objected to, so Batang Kali's 31 deaths, which an official report attributed mainly to heavy rain, are removed.

Correction: we now date the count of states that brought the 2022 forestry reforms into force to March 2025, when only Perlis and the Federal Territories had done so, instead of presenting it as current.

cards.big: Penang's city council approved a Tanjung Bungah tower the DOE had objected to. In October 2017, a landslide on the site killed 11 construction workers.
cards.sub: DOE can object, but planning power sits with states and their councils. By March 2025, most states had not adopted Parliament's 2022 forest reform.

cards.big: The word 'environment' is absent from the Federal Constitution. DOE can object but states can proceed regardless.
cards.sub: NFA enacted under Article 76(1)(b) to promote uniformity but states must voluntarily adopt under Article 76(3). Planning authorities can and do override DOE rejections.

cards.big: Satellite forest-loss estimates far exceed official figures, and Johor's largest excision was carried out secretly
cards.sub: 15,011 ha excised in 2014; state forestry couldn't justify it to auditors. Kedah logs Ulu Muda despite the federal ban; it supplies 80% of Penang's water.

cards.big: States resist NFA reforms because land conversion generates revenue that federal transfers don't replace
This isn't development versus environment. It's a system where states profit from conversion and the people who die are never the people who approve.
Like a building code that only applies in the lobby. Each floor sets its own rules, and nobody checks the wiring.
cards.sub: Federal environmental standards without state enforcement create a protection gap where disasters concentrate

cards.big: Either amend the Constitution to give DOE enforcement power, or make conservation more profitable than conversion through fiscal transfers
